title: Transformation in higher education cannot run on goodwill alone
summary: Bridgette Bewick and Sarah Hubbard argue that sustainable transformation in higher education depends on creating greater clarity about authority, responsibility, agency and what roles can realistically be expected to hold
full_text:
As universities navigate the complexity of financial pressure and restructuring, more and more responsibility is being carried through informal effort, initiative and care.

This is partly a story of doing more with less, but also about work changing shape. Roles are being reinterpreted in practice, while the agreements around authority, support, time and limits often remain implicit.

Under these conditions, the question of what roles can realistically hold becomes harder to avoid. A gulf often opens between what roles were previously able to contain and what they are now being asked to encompass, even as expectations continue to expand.

For many, this shows up in how their role is experienced day to day. This is not necessarily because anything formal has changed – job descriptions may remain intact, and structures may look broadly familiar. In practice, more depends on colleagues stepping in to connect, translate and absorb tension that does not quite sit anywhere else. None of this is new, and under pressure it becomes harder to ignore how much of it sits outside explicit agreement.

Transformation changes roles before organisations notice – work expands, boundaries shift, and new expectations emerge. The challenge is not that roles evolve. They always have. The challenge is whether those shifts become conscious and supported, or whether they are absorbed through goodwill alone.

What compassion and curiosity reveal

We made the case that transformation will only be sustainable if colleagues feel safe, supported, and connected to one another in the work, and that curiosity helps us stay with complexity rather than close it down too quickly.

But what do those commitments to compassion and curiosity ask of roles in practice?

Compassion and curiosity do not sit outside the system. They reshape it. They change what is noticed, what is responded to and what is taken up as someone’s responsibility. Without clarity about role, authority and responsibility, awareness can quietly become ownership, and concern can become an unspoken obligation.

One of the unintended consequences of compassionate and curious cultures is that more becomes visible. We notice distress, tension, inequity, exclusion, broken processes and emerging risks.

Noticing a problem does not create a contract to solve it. The ability to see what needs attention and the responsibility for taking action are not the same thing. When institutions blur this distinction, work expands through goodwill rather than agreement.

The issue is not invisible work. It is uncontracted work

As roles are adapted in response to changing demands, responsibility can begin to accumulate through action rather than explicit agreement. Work often gathers around those who are seen as dependable, who notice what needs attention, or for whom declining additional responsibilities carries a particular cost. This pattern frequently reflects existing inequalities in status, role, gender, race and contract type.

The challenge isn’t that work changes shape. It’s that new expectations emerge faster than conversations about authority, support, accountability and limits.

In the absence of explicit contracting, responsibility can expand by default rather than conscious agreement.

Colleagues are left navigating what has been noticed, what has been assumed and what has actually been agreed. The result is often less a problem of commitment than a problem of clarity. Contracting creates the opportunity for that clarity. Without this, responsibility expands through goodwill rather than design.

The challenge isn’t only practical. It’s emotional. Transformation asks us to work at the edge of what is known, established and familiar. As roles evolve, we often find ourselves carrying uncertainty alongside responsibility: navigating tensions, absorbing concerns and making judgements in situations where expectations are not always clear.

Alongside possibility and purpose can come frustration, doubt, loss and competing loyalties. These experiences are not signs that transformation is failing. They are part of what transformation feels like. The question is whether we acknowledge them and create conditions in which they can be worked with collectively rather than carried individually.

Power is not only structural

Discussions about invisible work often focus on power and rightly so. Existing hierarchies influence whose work we recognise, whose concerns we hear, and who is expected to absorb additional responsibility. Existing inequities continue to shape who can refuse, who feels able to challenge, and whose contribution remains invisible.

Yet power is not only structural. It is also personal.

Alongside questions of authority granted by the institution sit questions of authority claimed by us as individuals. Transformation requires power with others through collaboration and collective action, and power within ourselves; the capacity to exercise judgement, to set boundaries, to challenge assumptions, and to inhabit our role fully.

Sustainable transformation requires both. Our institutions need to provide authority, legitimacy and protection. We need to recognise and step into the discretion, expertise and agency we already possess. Waiting to be fully authorised can be as limiting as acting without support. Neither institutional permission nor personal agency is sufficient on its own.

Making responsibility discussable

Visibility alone does not redistribute work. We need conversations about ownership, authority, capacity and support.

The leadership task for all of us is to create clarity about what is being held, by whom, with what authority, and with what support. This requires greater awareness of how roles are shaped in practice. This might involve pausing within existing delivery and governance spaces to ask what is being progressed, and how the work is being shared.

That includes making redistribution visible. Where is responsibility gathering? Does that align with what has been agreed? Who is carrying work because they care rather than because it belongs to their role? Even brief conversations can change what becomes possible.

Without these conversations, work can be carried through goodwill, care and responsiveness without agreement about who it belongs to.

What is it acceptable to name?

Who is able to question how things work?

Who is labelled as difficult when they do?

These are not questions that sit outside roles. They are part of how roles are made possible. Without intentional distribution, fundamentally collective challenges continue to be carried as individual concerns.

Clarity is not simply about defining tasks. It involves creating shared understanding of what sits within a role, what sits outside of a role, and what requires collective ownership. Healthy boundaries are not a barrier to compassion. They are what make compassion sustainable. As roles evolve in response to changing conditions, these conversations matter because responsibility can otherwise expand by default, without authority, support or agreement.

This is especially true for relational, emotional, and interpretive work; work that enables institutions to continue to function and to realise the benefits of transformation yet often remains unaccounted for. Work cannot be sustained simply because it is acknowledged. It requires authority, permission, support and protection.

The work ahead

None of this is straightforward. It is not about doing more. It’s about noticing where work is already being done and how it is being carried. The question is not whether roles will continue to evolve – they will. The question is whether we consciously renegotiate what they can reasonably hold.

Compassion helps us notice what matters. Curiosity helps us stay open to complexity. Neither tells us automatically what should be carried, by whom, and at what cost.

Sustaining transformation requires clarity about responsibility, authority, support and limits. It requires institutions that provide permission and protection for individuals to act. It also requires us, as individuals, to step into the authority that already sits within our role.

The task is not to carry more. It is to become more conscious about what is being carried, who is carrying it, and whether that remains the right arrangement.

Practically, leaders and teams can ask four simple questions: What work has emerged that was never explicitly agreed? Who currently holds it? What authority accompanies that responsibility? And what needs to be shared, stopped or renegotiated? Transformation becomes more sustainable when these questions become routine rather than exceptional.

If transformation in higher education depends on colleagues stepping forward, responsibility cannot continue to accumulate through goodwill alone. It must become something that is consciously contracted, appropriately authorised, collectively owned and intentionally sustained.

The post Business, government and education leaders try to reinvent college from scratch appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
MONTPELIER, Vt. — All red brick and white trim and dating from as far back as the 1870s, the buildings that frame a grassy quad on a hill above Vermont’s capital city comprise the quintessential college campus.

Behind the scenes, this holdover from the 19th century is where a group of business, college and government leaders is working on the task of reinventing higher education for the 21st.

An entirely new college is being planned here to not only change how higher education is delivered, and at what price, but to highlight ways the current business model no longer works — yet is so deeply entrenched that the easiest way to fix it is to begin again from scratch.

Called the Greenway Institute — “green” as in new — the project will adopt instructional methods proven to work well, such as real-world training under the supervision of faculty mentors, while stripping away the frills, distractions and layers of bureaucracy that make college in America so expensive.

“It’s not fancy. It’s a place where you do have a meaningful relationship with your faculty members. But you also take out your own trash,” said Mark Somerville, the founding president.

Even more unexpected than the location of this startup is the timing. Other colleges and universities are closing or at risk of closing. In Vermont alone, seven private colleges have shut down in the last 10 years.

But Somerville, the former provost of Olin College of Engineering, said this “moment of mass extinction” makes it clearer than ever that “we need new models in higher ed.”

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Several other experimental higher education institutions are also in the planning stages — enough to have been newly organized in January by Duke University into a Future Universities Alliance, of which Greenway is a member.

Project Polymath, for instance — founded by Dan Futrell, former CEO of the Pat Tillman Foundation, which gives scholarships to military veterans — proposes to mentor bachelor’s degree students beginning in 2028 through three different majors each, then place them in apprenticeships with employers for two years. It calls itself an “ROTC for the private sector.”

There is “broad agreement that something has to change, and also recognition that changing legacy institutions from within is agonizingly difficult,” said Brian Rosenberg, former president of Macalester College, author of the book “‘Whatever It Is, I’m Against It’: Resistance to Change in Higher Education” and a member of both the Greenway and Polymath advisory boards.

These new projects, Rosenberg said, are “essentially an alternative to trying to change these institutions from within, which hasn’t been working very well.”

Greenway bought its campus in 2023 from the Vermont College of Fine Arts, which had mostly gone remote by then and would be acquired a year later by the California Institute of the Arts after enrollment declines and multimillion-dollar deficits.

Many renovations are complete, and the new school tentatively plans to open next fall. It’s raised $4.5 million toward a goal of $30 million by 2031, Somerville said — including a grant from the National Science Foundation, which it shared with partner institution Elizabethtown College in Pennsylvania. It’s also making money by renting out space it doesn’t need.

Greenway’s founders and advisers include tech executives, CEOs, a onetime Vermont state secretary of education, a NASA engineer and current and former administrators from Harvard, Dartmouth, Tufts and other schools. It will teach one subject: engineering.

Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is projected

The project already tested its model last year on a group of students borrowed from other schools, which gave them academic credit for coming to the Greenway campus and doing hands-on work with faculty supervisors in a prototype semester. Instead of sitting in conventional classes and lectures, the students designed wind turbines and solar-powered traffic signals.

“Basically, they learned electrical, mechanical and some controls by doing, versus somebody standing at the front and saying, ‘All right, you know, this is Norton’s equivalent theorem’ [of electronic circuits] that you’ll never use in your life,” said Troy McBride, co-founder of a Vermont-based solar panel manufacturer and chair of Greenway’s board of directors.

New research by scholars at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the Strada Education Foundation shows that work-based learning improves students’ likelihood of getting jobs, advancing in their careers and earning more than classmates who studied in other ways. But fewer than half of students at public four-year universities experience paid work-based learning, a separate Strada study showed. (Strada is among the funders of The Hechinger Report, which co-produced this story.)

“We’re stuck in the 1950s,” McBride said of traditional instruction. “We haven’t responded to the internet, let alone AI. We’re still memorizing things that don’t need to be memorized, and we’re not teaching skills and tools. We’re teaching facts, which is the least useful thing in these times.”

Jazz Gonzalez, who was part of Greenway’s prototype semester, said conventional lectures in his previous years in college left him wanting more.

Related: Threats of more closings have colleges and students worrying about how to save themselves

“A lot of the times they say, ‘This is the theory, this is how we usually apply it, and here you go, you’ll have an exam on it in a week,’ ” said Gonzalez, a Pennsylvania native who graduated in the spring from Elizabethtown. “I would always say, ‘OK, but how do I dig deeper into this? How do I use this, and how do I actually apply it to what I’m going to be doing in the future?’ ”

When Greenway is in full operation, students are expected to live on campus for two years doing projects, then go on to real-world workplaces for an additional two years while continuing to get support from faculty.

That lowers the cost to the college of providing housing. It’s also part of the educational strategy: Research shows that students who live on campus benefit from a communal setting for the first two years, according to the Association of College and University Housing Officers, with lower dropout rates than classmates who live off campus. But “by the time a student is in their junior year at most colleges, they’re, like, ‘Could I go study abroad now?’ ” Somerville said.

Greenway students will also shop and cook for themselves in communal kitchens, plan their own extracurricular activities and, if they want to go to the gym, sign up for the nearby Planet Fitness or other off-campus options.

It’s “very lean,” said Emmanuel Attah, an engineering major at Elizabethtown who was also part of Greenway’s prototype semester. He liked that, Attah said. “It goes right to the point. The students felt really in charge,” which he said was different from his previous experience in higher education.

Related: More than a quarter of private colleges are at risk of closing, new projection shows

Not having climbing walls or football games “really didn’t matter to us,” Gonzalez said.

Those kinds of amenities are among the factors driving up the cost of college. In the 10 years leading up to the pandemic, the consulting firm McKinsey found, spending on noninstructional services grew four times faster than spending on instruction. From 2012 to 2021, universities and colleges added facilities much faster than they added students, according to a separate study by the building consulting firm Gordian.

“You see tuition going up and up and up and up, and not necessarily for the reasons that a student would want them to go up, like a better educational experience,” McBride said. “A lot of it is for amenities, extras and for space sitting empty.”

Increasingly, said Somerville, “young people and their parents are looking at [college] and saying, ‘Does this actually make sense?’ ”

There’s another reason to make students responsible for cooking their own meals and scheduling their free time, said Annick Dewald, Greenway’s first faculty member: so they learn how.

“We assume that they can’t balance cooking for themselves and cleaning up for themselves, in addition to being college students, and I’m not totally sure why,” said Dewald, who teaches engineering.

“Employers have told me the hardest thing about fresh-from-college undergrads is getting them to show up on time or sleep eight hours at night or to figure out how to feed themselves,” she said. “That to me is a product of how we view college or what services we provide.”

Hannah Root, the project’s chief of staff, recounted taking the college’s “test” students food-shopping, which she called one of the most challenging moments of the prototype semester. There were “just so many real decisions that they were having to make that it was clear they hadn’t really experienced before,” such as whether or not to buy organic produce.

Without the frills, Greenway expects to charge an annual tuition of $25,000 or less, offset by what students would be paid for their in-person work — generally called “co-op” jobs by other universities and colleges that offer them. The average full-time co-op pays $25.42 an hour for juniors and $27.17 an hour for seniors, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers. That comes to more than $50,000 a year.

Related: As international enrollment falls, U.S. students face program cuts and higher prices

The average published total cost of attendance at private, nonprofit four-year universities is $65,470, College Board reports.

Greenway has to wait until it formally opens to apply for accreditation, a process that then takes at least four years. That’s one of the many examples of red tape that makes innovation challenging. It also means students won’t be eligible for federal grants or loans. Greenway’s founders said they expect the money they raise will offset that, and that accreditation would be retroactively applied to graduates’ degrees.

The plan is to grow to 500 students in Montpelier, half of them on campus at any given time, and to add other locations nationwide, Somerville said. For now, he said, Greenway needs about 370 students by 2031 to break even.

Inside College Hall at the center of the campus — four stories of iconic red-brick Second Empire-style architecture, with big arched windows and a mansard roof — the Greenway team has arranged color-coded sticky notes on a whiteboard listing the many steps it takes to start a college.

McBride pointed out the building’s big, well-lit classrooms.

“They’re perfect for work-based learning,” he said of how rooms on the 150-year-old campus are being repurposed. “Lots of big rectangular spaces. Lots of windows.”

Greenway may not be for everyone, said Rebecca Holcombe, former Vermont secretary of education and candidate for governor, and another founder.

It’s “for kids who really know what they want to do,” she said. “This is a great way to get there fast without having to pay for all the things that, frankly, you may never use or want to take advantage of.”

And while the particularly large number of closing colleges in Vermont may seem a bad omen for an effort to open a new one, Holcombe said experiencing the problem has made the state that much more focused on it.

“We’re ready to start saying, ‘OK, if not this, then what?’ ”

Contact writer Jon Marcus at 212-678-7556, jmarcus@hechingerreport.org or jpm.82 on Signal.

title: Are Scholarships Based on Country of Origin in Danger?
summary:
Are Scholarships Based on Country of Origin in Danger?
Johanna Alonso Tue, 09/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

Such scholarships are fairly common, though one international enrollment expert acknowledged that some institutions already had doubts about offering them.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
The Department of Justice is investigating Harvard University scholarships earmarked for Chinese students, raising questions about how similar funding at other institutions could be affected.

Earlier this summer, the DOJ wrote in a letter to Harvard that it had audited the university’s gifts from Chinese donors and uncovered funds designated for scholarships “with preference given to students from particular countries.” The department said it was investigating those scholarships and demanded further information about those donations, as well as details about the recipients of the scholarships.

The Trump administration has been scrutinizing foreign donations to universities since last year, arguing that such gifts raise concerns about national security and foreign influence over institutional research priorities. But the DOJ’s central concern in this case seems less about the source of the money than the fact that it is set aside for Chinese students, which the department wrote in its letter is a violation of Title VI, the statute that prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color and national origin in programs that receive federal funding.

“Harvard appears to be accepting these funds with restrictions and conditions from China-based sources and then providing this student financial aid with preference to foreign students based on their national origin, presumably Chinese, to the potential detriment of persons of other national origins including citizens of the United States,” reads the letter, signed by Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon. It includes an appendix listing 13 organizations that have apparently donated funds toward scholarships for Chinese students.

The rationale mirrors the Justice Department’s arguments disputing the legality of scholarships for members of other groups, including racial minorities and LGBTQ+ students. Since Trump came into office, the number of race-based scholarships has plummeted, as numerous institutions have reworked such awards to use race-neutral criteria instead.

But this is the first time the department has raised alarm about scholarships based on country of origin. The letter came two months after an organization calling itself the Global Philanthropy Accountability Project published a press release drawing attention to large donations from SOHO China Foundation, the charitable foundation of a massive Chinese real estate firm, to Harvard and Yale Universities. The donations were made in 2014; Yale’s press release at the time said the funds would provide scholarships to low-income Chinese students.

The DOJ lists the “Beijing SOHO China Urban Cultural Foundation”—which appears to be a longer version of the foundation’s name, according to internal documents—among the organizations in the appendix of its letter.

It is also unclear who is responsible for the Global Philanthropy Accountability Project; the press release quotes a principal researcher who is identified only as Steven. Inside Higher Ed reached out to two email addresses listed on the organization’s website, but both bounced back.

Beyond Harvard

Scholarships based on a student’s country of origin are much less common than those that include race as a criteria, according to Jackie Bright, president and CEO of the National Scholarship Providers Association.

Still, numerous colleges do offer scholarships to students from specific countriesc or regions. They range from small grants of a few hundred dollars to much more substantial awards, like the African Scholars program at Wesleyan University, which was launched in 2023 and offers a full ride to about 10 African students annually.

Many of these awards are funded by donations from international alumni, faculty members or other individuals with close ties to the university.

“A lot of times, these scholarships … [are drawn from] endowments that are created by private donors, often because they care about populations from their parts of the world to have access to education,” said Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators. “Most times it would be alumni or friends of the university that really feel that the way they can pay it forward is through scholarships that would provide and open up greater access to students who, many times, otherwise would not have access to those opportunities. So, it’s good for the students, it’s good for the institutions and it’s good for [the U.S.] when it comes to people-to-people exchange.”

Clay Harmon, executive director of AIRC: The Association of International Enrollment Management, said this isn’t the first time the legality of such scholarships has been called into question.

“It is a bit of a gray area. I do believe that every institution makes their own risk assessment and evaluation. There are many examples out there of scholarships intended for [students from a specific country] and so it seems like there’s a strong history of institutions feeling comfortable with that,” he said. “But I do know of particular public institutions or systems around the country that are very sensitive about this and are much more cautious.”

He added that he wouldn’t be surprised if institutions decided to make small tweaks to the scholarships’ criteria to avoid scrutiny. Instead of requiring recipients to have been born in a specific country, he suggested, perhaps the scholarship would be open to individuals who have a particular interest in the country or spent time living there.

According to Bright, it doesn’t look like any such scholarships have changed their language or criteria so far.

Only about 12.6 percent of international undergraduate students rely on institutional funding to pay for their studies, according to the Institute of International Education’s Open Doors report. But selective institutions with large endowments, like Harvard, often cover full financial need for both domestic and international students; Harvard specifically provides financial assistance to international students at a higher rate than to domestic students, according to a 2025 analysis by The Boston Globe.

Regardless, taking away opportunities for international students to fund their education further discourages them from studying in the U.S., Harmon said, adding to a long list of Trump administration actions that experts say are making the country a far less appealing destination.

title: 2-Year College ‘Extends Mission’ With 4-Year Degrees
summary:
2-Year College ‘Extends Mission’ With 4-Year Degrees
Joshua.Bay Tue, 09/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

Generations College is adding bachelor’s degrees, betting that students who might otherwise stop after an associate degree will keep going.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Kimberly Newson was 45 years old, married and a mother of six when she enrolled in an associate degree program at Generations College.

Her goal was to show her children that you’re never too old to start something new or pursue a degree. But as Newson approached graduation—and ultimately became her class valedictorian—she had already decided her college journey would end there.

That changed when the private nonprofit two-year institution in Chicago announced it would offer bachelor’s degrees for the first time in its 122-year history, starting this fall.

“I thought I was done. I even told my husband, ‘Yeah, I have my associate degree. I think I’m finished,’” Newson said. “My emails were flooded with so many schools reaching out to me, and I have not opened one.”

What changed her mind, Newson said, was the opportunity to continue at an institution where she had already built relationships and felt supported as an adult learner.

“I had already gained so much trust with Generations College,” she said. “They understand that parents, that adults that go back to school have so much on their plate, so many responsibilities, but they give you that encouragement and that push to keep going.”

Beyond the associate degree: Generations’ decision comes as a growing number of two-year colleges nationwide are expanding into four-year degrees, often with the goal of creating more affordable and accessible avenues to a bachelor’s degree. More than 200 community colleges across 24 states now offer at least 767 bachelor’s degree programs, even as some four-year institutions have pushed back against the expansion over concerns about competition and duplication.

Research suggests the programs may also be reaching students who otherwise would not pursue a four-year degree. One recent study found that community college bachelor’s degree graduates earned between $4,000 and $9,000 more annually than comparable associate degree graduates, and researchers found that many students enrolled in the programs had not previously considered pursuing a bachelor’s degree.

Grace Alexis, chancellor of Generations College, said the institution will offer four bachelor’s programs: business administration, business administration with an AI focus, entrepreneurship and entrepreneurship with an AI focus. She said the decision to add the degrees was driven in part by students who wanted to continue their education at Generations rather than transfer elsewhere after earning an associate degree.

“A lot of them go kicking and screaming. They don’t want to leave because they know that they’re not going to find the experience that they have at Generations at other schools,” Alexis said. “So, because of their many requests to continue their education with us, we felt that we had to remove the barrier.”

The bachelor’s programs will require 120 credits, compared with 60 for an associate degree. Alexis said students will also have access to the supports Generations already provides, including flexible scheduling, hybrid and online courses, and financial assistance, such as the college’s scholarship program for single parents.

The college said students in the bachelor’s programs will pay the same annual tuition rate as students pursuing associate degrees, though completing the bachelor’s requires an additional two years of study. The same financial aid opportunities available to associate degree students will also be available to bachelor’s students.

Generations initially planned to enroll 30 students in the bachelor’s programs this fall but is nearing 40, Alexis said. All students in the inaugural cohort are Generations alumni who previously earned an associate degree from the college. The college intentionally limited the first cohort to its own graduates as it builds out the programs, and it plans to expand enrollment in the spring, for which it is currently recruiting.

Alexis said the college chose to start with business administration and entrepreneurship because those programs already enroll a large share of Generations students.

“Generations College offers the oldest two-year program for business administration in the state of Illinois,” Alexis said. “The majority of our students are currently enrolled in business administration and entrepreneurship programs, so the need and demand was very clear to us.”

Extending the mission: For Generations, the expansion is a bet that allowing students to remain at the institution where they earned their associate degree—and maintain the relationships and supports they built there—can encourage some who might otherwise stop after an associate degree to continue toward a bachelor’s.

Alexis said the expansion does not mean Generations is moving away from its role as a two-year college. Instead, she sees the bachelor’s programs as an extension of that mission.

“We didn’t just think about doing this overnight. This was a plan that we had for probably over 10 years or so,” Alexis said. “We’re not abandoning our two-year mission. All that we’re doing is extending it.”

She cautioned other two-year institutions considering bachelor’s degrees against viewing the programs primarily as a way to boost enrollment.

“Sometimes the motive of the two-year colleges to add the four-year degree is to increase their enrollment, and I want to caution them in that,” Alexis said. “In our case, for example, we’re a small college. Our goal is not to become a large institution. If we become a large institution, it’s an outcome of what we’re doing, not that that is our goal. We want to become a more complete institution, as opposed to becoming a larger institution.”

For Newson, who is enrolled this fall in the business administration program with an AI focus, the opportunity to continue at Generations has already changed the trajectory of her own education.

“You never know what opening up a bachelor’s program to other people means,” Newson said. “Sometimes people can be complacent with, ‘OK, I was comfortable with this institution, so since they only have an associate degree program, I’m not going to move forward,’ and they may just leave it there. But if you open it up to them, they can achieve so much.”

title: University of Pennsylvania Now Enforcing Math Prerequisites
summary:
University of Pennsylvania Now Enforcing Math Prerequisites
Emma Whitford Tue, 09/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

As college students’ math skills decline worldwide, Penn is verifying students’ readiness for advanced calculus and algebra courses.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
Starting this fall, the University of Pennsylvania will require students to satisfy prerequisite requirements for six advanced calculus and algebra courses. The change comes as college officials across the country are working to address incoming students’ declining math skills.

Penn’s math prerequisites aren’t new; they have always been listed alongside course descriptions in the catalog, but now the university will verify them instead of relying on students to decide whether or not they meet the requirements, according to Molly McGlone, deputy dean of undergraduate studies in the College of Arts & Sciences.

“Faculty in Math and other disciplines have carefully designed the courses in a sequential manner to support student learning. Students who are in courses that they are not adequately prepared for can often run into challenges,” McGlone told Inside Higher Ed in an email.

Students can satisfy the prerequisite requirements by taking a corresponding Penn math course, receiving a relevant Advanced Placement credit or passing a credit exam. Credit exams are held during new student orientation and once again when the semester starts, according to The Daily Pennsylvanian, which first reported the news. Students who enroll in one of the six targeted courses but don’t meet the prerequisite requirements may see a registration issue flag on their schedule.

Math prerequisites are common, but the types of prerequisites colleges employ and how strictly they enforce them has changed over the years, said Pamela Burdman, founder and executive director of Just Equations, a California-based math education–equity nonprofit.

“Many college systems have moved away from remedial prerequisites that require students to repeat high school content in favor of corequisite strategies in which students take a college-level course with extra support,” she told Inside Higher Ed in an email. “Research has shown that many students were being placed into courses lower than the courses where they have the capacity to succeed.”

Penn’s change is how colleges typically approach a standard undergraduate math sequence—several calculus courses, linear algebra and differential equations, Burdman said. Just one in five students who take calculus in high school will enroll directly in Calc II, according to research by David Bressoud, professor emeritus at Macalester College and former president of the Mathematical Association of America. Meanwhile, most students who take high school calculus will repeat it in college, take a lower-level math course or a math course that doesn’t require calculus at all, such as business math, Burdman said.

“In general, more selective colleges would like STEM majors to have taken calculus if it’s available to them, or at least be ready to take calculus when they start college,” she said. “At the same time, there is growing awareness that access to calculus can depend on what high school a student attends, and Black and Latinx students generally have less access to calculus courses. So increasingly colleges are making available at least precalculus courses as an on-ramp to calculus.”

Math achievement has been declining nationally, Burdman noted. A report from the University of California, San Diego, made national and international headlines in November when it stated that the number of first-year students whose math skills fell below a middle school level had increased nearly 30-fold over the past five years. Since then, hundreds of University of California system math professors have called on the system to bring back standardized testing requirements for admission.

“While pandemic-era disruptions accelerated this trend, it began before COVID,” Burdman said of the decline in math skills. “Experts believe other long-term trends are at play—such as absenteeism, effects of social media and students’ use of AI.”

title: August Cuts to Start the Academic Year
summary:
August Cuts to Start the Academic Year
Josh Moody Tue, 09/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

Harvard University cut more than 100 jobs last month amid a lengthy restructuring process. Multiple others also enacted smaller cuts.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
With new fiscal and academic years underway, only a small number of colleges announced layoffs, buyouts and related staffing moves last month, though a couple enacted significant cuts.

Even the rich weren’t immune to layoffs; Harvard University cut more than 100 jobs in August, following layoffs in July as well. Elsewhere, colleges enacted smaller cuts, hiring freezes and voluntary separation programs to address budget gaps attributed to declining enrollments and rising operating costs.

Harvard University

The nation’s wealthiest institution laid off at least 100 employees in a wave of August cuts, concluding a monthslong administrative restructuring of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The private university cut 165 jobs altogether as part of the restructuring, with 100 of those coming last month, The Harvard Crimson reported. Some employees were offered new or reconfigured roles amid the reorganization, which aims to close a $350 million structural deficit.

Harvard officials wrote in a message to campus that the cuts amounted to “a series of painful decisions, the effects of which will continue to be felt across our community.” Now that layoffs are complete, officials noted some affected employees may take new roles amid the overhaul.

Minnesota State University, Mankato

Grappling with a projected $22 million budget deficit, MSU-Mankato is making dozens of cuts.

The public university plans to shed about 60 faculty and staff jobs in total, The Minnesota Star Tribune reported. While Mankato plans to lay off 17 employees, the majority of the cuts will reportedly come through the elimination of vacant positions and early-retirement incentives.

Mankato President Edward Inch said in a video announcing the cuts that costs have continued to rise while tuition revenue and state support have remained sluggish, necessitating changes to ensure the financial stability of the university. The cuts come ahead of a steep tuition hike: The state system plans to increase tuition by an average of 6.25 percent by next school year.

Baker University

The private university in Kansas completed a round of cuts over the summer that included laying off 21 staff members and freezing hiring for 27 vacant positions, The Baker Orange reported.

President Jody Fournier told the newspaper that the cuts are the result of an analysis that began in the spring and were necessary to balance staffing levels amid declining enrollment and revenues. Beyond the layoffs, Fournier said that he and other administrators also took pay cuts.

Columbia College Chicago

Officials at the private college announced another round of layoffs last month.

“As a part of our continued work to align Columbia’s operating structure with our current enrollment and fiscal realities, we have made additional staff reductions,” President Shantay N. Bolton wrote in an Aug. 21 message to the campus community. “This week, some colleagues were notified that their positions have been eliminated. These actions represent the reductions currently planned and include vacant positions that will not be filled.”

Though Bolton did not specify the number of jobs cut, the United Staff of Columbia College union told The Columbia Chronicle that 14 of its members were among those included in the latest cuts. The college has had several rounds of layoffs in the last two years as administrators seek to plug a persistent budget deficit amid declining enrollment. In May, the college announced that it had paused faculty sabbaticals for a second straight year as part of ongoing cost-cutting efforts.

Officials have said the college’s budget deficit could surpass $40 million.

Northwestern University

In reconfiguring its Program of African Studies, Northwestern cut two staff jobs.

The program will move from the Office of Research to the Office of the Provost, where faculty will continue to conduct research and teach classes, officials told Inside Higher Ed. The program, founded in 1948, will continue to award undergraduate and graduate degrees in African studies.

Officials said the move will “re-energize” the program and “ensure its success going forward.”

Brookdale Community College

Administrators at the New Jersey college announced plans to lay off employees to offset enrollment declines and rising costs, but have not publicly specified how many jobs may be cut.

BCC’s Board of Trustees approved a reduction in force last month. The local Asbury Park Press noted that rising health-care costs are part of the impetus behind the cuts; officials told the newspaper that the cost of employee health benefits jumped $11 million year over year, prompting the college to “make difficult decisions now” to ensure long-term fiscal sustainability.

Heartland Community College

Trustees at the two-year college in Illinois approved a voluntary separation-incentive plan last month that they expect to yield an annual $1.5 million in savings, The Pantagraph reported.

Though 88 employees are eligible, administrators project 30 to 35 will take buyouts.

Officials said at a meeting last month the buyout plan is proactive and intended to respond to long-term challenges on the horizon rather than immediate financial needs. HCC is seeking to reduce personnel costs, which comprise more than 70 percent of operating expenditures.

title: The Ticks and Leeches of Higher Education
summary:
The Ticks and Leeches of Higher Education
kjohnsonbowles… Tue, 09/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

External culprits eating the sector alive by exploiting, capitalizing and profiting off higher education and students stand to weaken and kill it.

Byline(s)
Kathy Johnson Bowles
full_text:
Student loan lenders, investment firms and banks feed off higher education and its students, much like ticks and leeches who feed on the blood of other animals—slowly infecting and weakening the body. These industries act as an extraction pipeline by charging higher and higher interest rates and fees on student loans, overseeing investments and providing debit services at an unsustainable rate. The compounding effect of these industries is deleterious to the health of higher education and its ability to serve students.

The Federal Student Aid FY2024 Annual Report from the U.S. Department of Education illuminates the issues. The U.S. student loan market was valued at approximately $2.8 trillion in 2024, with federal loans comprising roughly 90 percent of the total portfolio. The Federal Student Aid office, the primary federal lender, paid approximately $2 billion to legacy Federal Family Education Loan program lenders in FY2024 for interest and special allowance subsidies. Federal Direct loan interest rates rose to 6.53 percent for undergraduates and 8.08 percent for graduate students in 2024–25, up sharply from the pandemic-era low of 2.75 percent in 2020–21.

Private student loans constitute a smaller but growing segment; the private market was valued at approximately $12 billion and is projected to reach $21 billion by 2032 at a 6.5 percent compound annual growth rate (CAGR). Major private lenders include Sallie Mae, Citizens Bank, SoFi, Earnest and College Ave. Sallie Mae, the largest private lender, reported net revenue of approximately $1.6 billion in fiscal 2023. The overall student loan market is projected to grow at approximately 8-9 percent CAGR through 2033, powered by rising borrowing demand and the accumulated cost burden on students rather than attributing growth solely to rising tuition.

Investment companies are among the largest endowment managers for colleges and universities. Firms such as BlackRock, Vanguard, Fidelity and TIAA-CREF manage substantial portions of higher education endowment assets. Historically, TIAA has been the leading retirement and investment provider specifically for the higher education workforce.

The endowment managers make their money by charging management and administrative fees (generally between 0.35 and 2 percent of an endowment’s total asset value annually). In some cases where endowments are heavily invested in hedge funds and private equity, managers may also extract incentive fees of 15 to 20 percent of investment profits. Fees vary significantly depending on the size of the endowment, asset classes and whether funds are managed internally or outsourced.

Most colleges and universities target at least a 7 to 9 percent annual return on investments to ensure an annual available spend (3 to 6 percent), which impacts the operating budget, with the remaining percentage returned to the corpus to ensure growth. In doing so, the amount paid to management firms can be massive.

On May 22, 2024, Alex Richwine and Dean Baker wrote, “University Endowment Returns Don’t Measure Up” for the Center for Economic and Policy Research. They explained what’s known as the Yale model, pioneered in the 1980s by the late Yale CFO David Swensen, who championed increased investments in hedge funds and private equity: “Swensen was adamant about tailoring the endowment approach to the particular institution. He warned that many endowment funds that try to imitate Yale will ‘end up with bloated, fee-driven investment management businesses,’ and that is precisely what happened.”

Emphasizing the problem of fees related to the Yale model, the authors note, “The relationship of today’s large endowment funds to hedge funds should raise serious questions. The hedge funds that help manage many endowment portfolios charge exorbitant fees, and it is not clear their services are worth the bill.”

“A simple example will illustrate the stakes. If a university hands over $1 billion of its endowment to be managed by a hedge fund with a 1.5 percent charge plus performance fees, it is giving away $15 million a year to someone who may be losing the endowment money.”

Finally, how do banks and private lenders prey on higher education and students? Three main avenues include student loans and securitization, campus partnerships and student accounts, and institutional services and debit services, as explained by a ProtectBorrowers.org article. After federal loans and grants, institutional aid (scholarships), and family contributions, students often have funding gaps, which are filled by private lenders, who charge higher interest rates than federal loans and charge origination fees. The lender often bundles loans and sells student loan asset–backed securities, in which it profits from underwriting and management fees.

In addition, Protect Borrowers (formerly the Student Borrower Protection Center) explains, while banks often pay universities royalties for exclusive rights to market credit cards, checking accounts and student debit cards, the cost is borne by students. Some universities outsource financial aid refunds to partner banks. Students who use these linked accounts frequently incur overdraft fees, monthly maintenance fees and out-of-network ATM fees. Every time a student swipes their co-branded debit or credit card, the bank collects a percentage of the transaction (interchange fee) from the merchant.

Additionally, investment banks underwrite municipal bonds to fund construction projects such as dormitories, stadiums and academic centers. Banks profit by taking a cut for facilitating the debt and selling interest rate swaps to the universities. Banks also handle the day-to-day liquidity of colleges and universities by processing deposits (e.g., student payments and contributions) and payments (e.g., vendor payments), for which the banks charge fees.

The banking industry is profiting, in part, from higher education. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s Quarterly Banking Profile: Fourth Quarter 2024 reported that FDIC-insured banks and savings institutions reported full-year 2024 net income of $268.2 billion, a 5.6 percent increase from 2023’s $256.9 billion. The industry’s return on assets increased to 1.12 percent for 2024, up three basis points from 2023. The American Bankers Association Banking Journal’s “Quarterly Banking Profile: Banking net income nearly $257B in 2023,” published on March 7, 2024, highlights the gains: Net operating revenue for the banking sector exceeded $1 trillion for the first time on record in 2023.

Philanthropic giving by corporations like JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and Citigroup’s foundations typically supports program enhancements, event sponsorships, capital projects, research initiatives and some scholarships. Although valuable, these arguably transactional gifts (corporations receive material benefits, such as recognition, naming rights and research results that can be monetized) may not materially affect college and university operating budgets. First, the gift is often restricted to a single purpose. Second, gifts can add to the operating budget because they may be one-time, while the cost to sustain a program or facility long term is borne by the institution.

title: Trump Attacks Academia—and Grad Students Ask if It’s Worth Saving
summary:
Trump Attacks Academia—and Grad Students Ask if It’s Worth Saving
Elizabeth Redden Tue, 09/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

It’s not just the federal government that’s telling grad students their work doesn’t matter.

Byline(s)
Lauren Chambers
JP Flores
full_text:
Earlier this year, atmospheric science Ph.D. student Lily Zhang published a letter explaining why she was leaving academia. She hadn’t failed. She hadn’t burned out. She had simply looked clearly at the system surrounding her work—the misogyny, the exploitation, the demand for total sacrifice with no guarantee of return—and decided it wasn’t worth it. As current and recent Ph.D. students ourselves, we recognize her story not as an exception but as emblematic of what it means to be a graduate student in 2026.

The current moment in American science is genuinely alarming. The Trump administration has doggedly attacked our nation’s top universities. The National Science Foundation’s board was disbanded this April. Federal research funding is contracting, with fewer grants awarded and widespread uncertainty about what comes next. Universities are cutting or pausing Ph.D. admissions. Postdoctoral job losses have surged nearly threefold. More than 10,000 STEM Ph.D.–trained scientists left federal roles in a single year. Those who remain are being told to develop a “plan B.” The message from Washington is blunt and repeated: Research is expendable.

But here is what that framing misses: The funding crisis isn’t breaking graduate students’ faith in academia. Graduate students had already been losing that faith for years, and the current crisis makes the problem impossible to keep ignoring.

Long before the first grant was frozen, graduate students were noticing a quieter set of contradictions. They were told that teaching matters while watching excellent teachers struggle for recognition. They were encouraged to engage with the public while learning that public scholarship rarely counts toward career advancement. They were told that mentorship is central to academic culture while watching faculty who pour themselves into students get passed over for colleagues with longer publication lists. They entered science hoping to improve society and discovered that the system rewards productivity more reliably than it rewards care.

As early-career academics ourselves, we’ve seen these patterns play out across academic disciplines. One of us—Lauren—wrote her own disciplinary farewell years ago: a breakup letter with astronomy. She had excelled in the field and was building a promising career. Yet she left because she could no longer swallow working in a field that made the work she wanted to do impossible—a system that refused “to acknowledge the terrestrial effects of celestial research.” Drawing on her training in African American studies, she pivoted into interdisciplinary social science, and today Lauren is at the Berkeley School of Information studying technology experts who work in advocacy and mission-driven nonprofit spaces. Still a scientist, but centering people and social problems.

The other, JP, stayed the course. He completed a Ph.D. in computational biology, mentored students, built public-facing science programs and entered the job market just as the research infrastructure began to unravel in 2025. He now holds two things at once: genuine belief in the power of scientific discovery, and serious doubts about whether the institutions responsible for supporting that discovery are willing to care for the people who sustain it.

Two different choices, but the same underlying question: Can a generation of scientists continue to devote their lives to institutions that no longer seem willing to invest in them?

What we see in ourselves and our peers is not a generation that lacks dedication or resilience. It is a generation that has looked at the contract academia offers—sacrifice now, security never, values optional—and begun asking whether it is worth signing. The current funding crisis has made that question urgent, but the question was already there.

To be sure, many scientists continue to do meaningful, ethical work inside imperfect institutions. And not every department is the same. But when talented, committed scientists leave academia not because they failed, but because they see its contradictions clearly, the problem is no longer individual. It is institutional.

The hardest question for faculty, administrators and department chairs is not what to do about Washington. It is what to do about the institutional culture already built and maintained. Promotion systems that treat mentorship as service and public scholarship as extracurricular. Evaluation structures that count citations and grant dollars but have no metric for the graduate students you helped retain. Department norms that ask junior scholars, and disproportionately scholars from historically marginalized groups, to carry the relational labor that holds communities together while counting none of it toward their advancement.

The federal government is telling researchers their work doesn't matter. This is a crisis worth fighting against. But if the institutions that researchers turn to for solidarity are the same ones that have spent decades telling them their values don't matter, that fight will be very hard to sustain.

Graduate students are not abandoning academia. They are asking whether the academy, as it is currently structured, deserves their trust. That is not a political question; it is an institutional one. And it is one that universities cannot afford to leave unanswered.

title: School uniform costs hit families, say charities
summary: New government rules limit the number of branded items schools can ask students to wear.
full_text:
Charities in Sussex have warned new school uniform costs could add financial pressure on struggling families.

This is despite new rules limiting the number of branded items state schools can require, which the government says will save parents money.

Children's charity Pelican Parcels, in Brighton and Hove, said it was set to double its school uniform support by the end of 2026 in response to "rising local demand".

"Every child deserves to start the school year feeling confident, with school uniform and shoes that fit properly," said head of operations Elaine Bailey. "For many families, the cost of uniform can be overwhelming."

The charity, which provides school uniforms, PE kits and supplies, said it gave more than 3,400 items to 520 children across 12 schools last year.

It is seeking donations of good-quality, unbranded uniform items, including polo shirts, pinafores and PE shorts.

Elsewhere, Horsham Matters, a charity in West Sussex, estimates that every school year, parents spend £336 on kitting out children for primary school, rising to £439 for secondary school.

Its chief executive Kelvin Glen said: "Nobody wants to send their child into a new classroom without everything they need to learn effectively.

"There is copious evidence that poverty during school years has a lasting impact on children's educational attainment and life chances."

The government policy, which came into effect from 1 September, restricts mandatory uniform items with school logos to three for primary schools and four for secondary schools, with the latter including ties.

Charlie Milner-Smith, in Worthing, said he had seen school items become more expensive with his son moving up a year at school.

"School shoes are definitely a lot more than they have been and kids grow out of them quickly – it's not just a one-off purchase," he said.

He sees the new rules as a good thing: "It stops you having to keep up with trends and makes sure your kids can just wear more generic things."

Steph Savage, from Surrey, can see the new rules helping with costs for her two children.

She told the BBC she had just made an order, and despite already owning some uniform, spent £250. This did not include branded items.

"It's quite a lot to ask from parents to buy all the uniform and school-specific stuff as well – that all adds up," Savage said.

Meanwhile, Lucy Smith, mother of two, said her children's school had been "quite easy-going".

"If our kids walked in without any branded uniform there'd be no questions asked anyway, so it's not made much of a difference to our family," she added.

In a statement from the Department for Education, a spokesperson said limiting branded items would give families breathing space and save some parents up to £50 per child.

It said it was supporting schools with new guidance to take steps to bring down costs for individual items, while "keeping more money in the pockets of hardworking families".

title: Travis Kelce’s $1.5M nonprofit faces scrutiny over management spending
summary: Travis Kelce’s Eighty-Seven and Running Foundation is facing scrutiny over its reported spending between 2021 and 2024. The nonprofit raised $1.5 million and spent about $1.1 million, with $469,000 listed for management and $446,000 for charity. Kelce’s business manager Aaron Eanes disputed the figures, saying some charitable operational costs were misclassified. He said management fees dropped to zero in 2025 as the foundation works to improve transparency and governance.
full_text:
Travis Kelce(Image via Getty Images)

Earlier this year, Travis Kelce’s reputation for giving back was facing a setback after an investigation into the NFL players’ charitable foundations raised questions about how some donated money was spent. Kelce’s Eighty-Seven and Running Foundation raised more than $1.5 million between 2021 and 2024, yet its reported charity spending was notably lower than that of several other NFL-linked organizations.

Travis Kelce nonprofit spending comes under scrutiny

In January, 2026, according to federal tax records examined by The Arizona Republic, Eighty-Seven and Running reported about $1.5 million in revenue during the three-year period and roughly $1.1 million in expenses. About $446,000 was listed under charitable spending, while $469,000 was reported as management costs. That works out to about 41 cents of every dollar spent going toward charity based on the filings. Charity Navigator generally views nonprofits spending at least 70 cents of each dollar on programs as efficient, while CharityWatch uses 75 cents as a benchmark for high efficiency. The figures have drawn attention partly because of the foundation's ties to A&A Management Group. The company was co-founded by Travis Kelce’s longtime business managers, Aaron and André Eanes. Aaron Eanes also serves as the nonprofit’s executive director. Laurie Styron, executive director of CharityWatch, raised concerns about the structure after reviewing the records. “It appears to function more as an extension of the management company versus as an independent public charity,” said Laurie Styron, the executive director of CharityWatch, an independent charity watchdog group that reviewed the nonprofit’s tax filings for The Arizona Republic. “That’s not how charities work. It’s wrong.”

Travis Kelce foundation says tax filings were incorrect

Travis Kelce’s team disputes the picture presented by the filings. Aaron Eanes said the reported figures did not properly classify some operational expenses tied to charitable work. “Operational costs for charitable efforts were “mistakenly reported under management rather than allocated adequately to program services,” Eanes told The Republic, so the public records do not provide an accurate “indication of where the resources were truly directed.”. Eanes said the foundation has since changed its approach, adding that management fees fell sharply in 2024 and reached zero in 2025. He also said the organization plans to expand its board, bring in nonprofit advisers and improve its reporting practices.

“Looking ahead, we are expanding our board of directors, bringing on advisers with nonprofit expertise, and restructuring our reporting processes to better reflect our actual program work. We are dedicated to ensuring this foundation operates at the highest standards.” The scrutiny comes as the NFL continues to highlight charitable work through the Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year program. Kelce has been nominated three times and has supported causes in both Kansas City and his hometown of Cleveland. His foundation’s reported numbers do not erase that community work, but they do highlight why financial transparency matters. For celebrity-led nonprofits, public trust depends not only on how much money is raised, but also on how clearly and responsibly that money reaches the people it is meant to help.

title: Centre of Excellence for Tribal students in A.P.’s Marikavalasa to provide competitive exam coaching
summary: The Centre has adopted a co-educational format on the lines of Eklavya Model Residential Schools, while providing separate dormitories and classrooms for boys and girls, besides CCTV cameras, dedicated wardens and enhanced security arrangements
full_text:
The State government on Sunday (August 30, 2026) said that it had established a Centre of Excellence (CoE) at the Residential School (RS-B) in Marikavalasa to provide intensive coaching to Scheduled Tribe (ST) students preparing for the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and the Indian Institutes of Technology Joint Entrance Examination (IIT-JEE), with the aim of increasing their representation in premier educational institutions. The remark comes at a time when controversy is brewing over the shifting of the residential school in Marikavalasa.

Andhra Pradesh Tribal Welfare Residential Educational Institutions Society (APTWREIS) secretary, M. Gowthami, visited the Centre on Sunday and inspected the classrooms. She described the initiative as a “historic decision” by the State government and said a CoE had been sanctioned for the Tribal Welfare Department on the lines of similar centres functioning under the Backward Classes and Social Welfare Departments.

The Centre has a sanctioned intake of 600 Intermediate students, comprising 300 boys and 300 girls, selected through a merit-based process. Physics Wallah, Noida, has been engaged as the coaching agency following a request-for-proposal process. Eighteen faculty members have been deputed and classes have commenced, she said.

Ms. Gowthami said Marikavalasa was chosen because of Visakhapatnam’s position as an educational hub and considerations relating to transport and other facilities for students from the North Andhra agency and plain areas. She said the Centre had adopted a co-educational format on the lines of Eklavya Model Residential Schools, while providing separate dormitories and classrooms for boys and girls, besides CCTV cameras, dedicated wardens and enhanced security arrangements.

As part of the transition, students earlier enrolled at RS (B), Marikavalasa, were shifted in a phased manner: 232 to the School of Excellence (Girls), Marikavalasa; 77 to APSWREIS institutions at Srikrishnapuram, Sabbavaram and Devarapalli; and 136 to APTWR institutions of their choice. Ms. Gowthami said students were shifted by bus under teachers’ supervision, with parents informed in advance and a farewell organised. She denied allegation that the campus had been vacated overnight.

Amid ongoing protests by tribal organisations and parents seeking continuation of the residential school at Marikavalasa, Minister of Tribal Welfare and Women and Child Welfare Gummidi Sandhya Rani said the Centre had been established at the instance of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, with the objective of improving educational standards among ST students and increasing their representation in premier educational institutions.

Ms. Sandhya Rani said 445 students of the Marikavalasa residential school had been shifted in phases without interruption to their education. She said 411 students were already studying at various schools, while alleging that some opposition leaders and tribal organisations were influencing the remaining 34 students and their parents, thereby affecting their education.

She appealed against politicising the education and future of tribal children. She said the government’s objective was to prepare ST students for national-level competitive examinations and provide them opportunities to seek admission to institutions such as the IITs, NITs, AIIMS and medical colleges.

title: Three takeaways from Voyage’s latest US outbound student report
summary:
Voyage's latest report draws on 48 months of Google search data and thousands of real student conversations captured, offering a fresh perspective on what US students are actively searching for, alongside what they are actually discussing.

The post Three takeaways from Voyage’s latest US outbound student report appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The US outbound market is correcting, not collapsing

Search interest in overseas study peaked in November 2024 – coinciding with Donald Trump’s re-election – and remained elevated for around a year. In 2026, it has eased back — but not to pre-2024 levels.

Average monthly searches across 17 destinations were 144.8K during the period of elevated interest, compared with 117,300 in 2026 year-to-date. The post-Covid normal was 114,700.

“The US is a large and shifting source market, and 2026 is a year of correction rather than crisis,” according to Voyage.

If 2026 stabilises around current levels, the US could be establishing a new, higher normal for outbound study interest rather than simply reverting to the pre-2024 pattern.

Japan has overtaken the UK, while South Korea has overtaken Germany

Between January and July 2026, Japan became the second most searched study destination among US students, overtaking the UK. South Korea also surpassed Germany, moving into fourth place.

Neither destination achieved this through outright growth. Search volumes across the top ten destinations were down year on year.

Japan was down 11.2%, compared with a 29.9% decline for the UK. South Korea was down 13.8%, compared with 21.7% for Germany.

“Canada remains dominant and resilient, while the Anglophone incumbents built on the highest volumes are declining fastest… the destinations gaining relative share are East Asian, and Japan’s rise is the clearest competitive signal,” according to the report.

The reasons students are looking abroad are more diverse and increasingly unrelated to rankings

The social data identifies six distinct prospective-student profiles in the US market: the Career Migrant, Escape-Driven Relocator, Prestige Strategist, Funding Chaser, Experience Seeker and Heritage Reconnector. They are not mutually exclusive, but represent different centres of gravity in student motivation and rankings are only central to one of them.

The Prestige Strategist is explicitly focused on credential value, rankings and whether a foreign qualification will be recognised by US employers. But the other profiles are motivated by very different considerations: migration, affordability and funding, safety and quality of life, social experience, or cultural and family connections.

That broader picture is also visible in the themes dominating student conversations. US prospective students over-index on Government & Policy, Student Logistics, Quality of Life and Community, while Education Outcomes and Services & Support sit below the global prospective-student benchmark.

Different students are looking abroad for fundamentally different reasons and the fastest-growing motivations in the market are not necessarily about university rankings or academic prestige.
